claim: The Knowledge Project #1, transcript PDF read in full (15 pages). Intuition is broadly overestimated and works in stable linear environments; experience is not expertise (Northcraft); Kahneman's disciplined intuition means starting with the base rate and then layering intuition; deliberate practice needs feedback; whether poker-style probability training transfers to complex decisions is an open question; a junior employee should first ask whether the organization is the right one, then offer another way to do it and run a low-cost, time-limited experiment; computers are good at large data and base rates and he is more optimistic than pessimistic about algorithms taking over tasks; Colonel Blotto: the stronger side simplifies the game, the weaker side adds battlefields; in a 2007 World Series family bet he offered to pay $20 if the Red Sox swept and receive $5 if not, put the sweep chance at 12-18%, and paid when they swept; influential books named: Rappaport's Creating Shareholder Value, Waldrop's Complexity (on the founding of the Santa Fe Institute), E. claim: Interview by Adam Grant on The Success Equation. Luck is what is out of your control; paradox of skill: as skill improves, luck becomes more important in determining outcomes (Gould's explanation of why no one has hit .400 since 1941: everyone has gotten better, so the spread of skill has narrowed); a good metric has persistence and predictive value (on-base percentage over batting average); in stiff competition look for differential skill or attack with an unusual tactic as the underdog; placing a problem on a continuum from stable and linear to unstable and non-linear is the fundamental first question; ambivalent about telling entrepreneurs the base rate because a few outsized winners need drive; calls combining academic rigor with practice the most satisfying part of his work; organizational habits are hard to unlearn; separating individual from team contribution is super difficult.

limitations: Edited article, not a verbatim transcript. Dated 2013, before his AI-era writing.

claim: Excess Returns episode with Kai Wu (The Intangible Economy), full transcript. The OpenAI forecast implies a 108% compound annual growth rate that no company in his reference class (U.S. public firms since 1950 starting at $2-5 billion of revenue, about 18,900 firm-years) had achieved; OpenAI's 2025 revenue was about $13 billion, 250% growth, in his words well ahead of expectations; 'unprecedented' is not 'impossible', not the base case but worth some probability; he triangulates with a bottoms-up build-up, the Bass diffusion model and base rates; base rates are living and breathing distributions; frontier LLMs are three to six similar models, 'it doesn't feel like a network-effect business to me'; AI is a sustaining innovation for Google, and the threat to search has not completely happened yet; almost all the value ends up with consumers because of competition (Brandenburger-Stuart); Nvidia's customers are developing their own technology; huge commitments must be made before the economics are known; cites an Economist estimate of about 25% of AI data centers delayed in 2025 and 30-50% in 2026 and says he does not know if it is right; intangible-heavy firms have similar averages but fatter tails (Enron: 61% compounded growth 1995-2000, bankrupt within nine months); proprietary software does not diffuse (Bessen); none of the laws of economics have been repealed; Walmart had negative free cash flow for its first 15 listed years and was a fabulous investment; intangible investment is about 1.5 times tangible, versus 1.4 times the other way in the late 1970s; the top ten U.S. public companies hold about a third of market value and about two thirds of economic profit; AI talent pay is largely equity tied to private up rounds.
